title: The Jewish people
hookLine: John Paul II visited Rome's synagogue in 1986 and spoke of elder brothers

lines: A POPE CROSSES A SHORT DISTANCE.
IN A CERTAIN WAY, ELDER BROTHERS.
cards: The synagogue of Rome stands by the Tiber, a short way from the Vatican. In 1986, Pope John Paul the Second crossed that short distance and went in, as a guest. Rome's chief rabbi, Elio Toaff, welcomed him.
The two men stood side by side before the congregation. And the pope spoke to the Jewish people in front of him as his brothers, his dearly loved brothers, and, in a certain way, his elder brothers.

teach.h: A SPIRITUAL BOND WITH ABRAHAM'S STOCK.
teach.b: You met Nostra Aetate back on day seven hundred ninety-five. It's where the pope's words came from. The council's declaration spoke of a spiritual bond linking the Church with the stock of Abraham.
It said the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people with whom God made the ancient covenant.
It also deplored hatred, persecutions and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews at any time and by anyone.

teach.h: THE GIFTS AND THE CALLING OF GOD.
teach.b: A verse the council leaned on: Paul, writing to the Romans about his own people, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance."
The council drew from this that God does not take back his gifts or his call. Later Catholic teaching put it plainly: the old covenant has never been revoked. Why elder?
In a family, the elder sibling was there first.

The pope's word carried both closeness and humility: Christians come after, and owe a debt. He also recalled the long history of suffering, and repeated the council's words deploring hatred and persecution.

Jews understand their covenant and their life on their own terms, not as part of a Christian story. Some Jewish readers have welcomed the phrase; others have noted that in Genesis, elder brothers don't always fare well.
Both reactions are part of the conversation.

teach.h: A WEEK OF NEIGHBORS, AND THE ROOT.
teach.b: Look back at the week: the Holy See, canon law, spiritual ecumenism, Anglicans, Lutherans, other Christians.
Today the circle reaches past the churches entirely, to the people whose olive tree, in Paul's image, Christians were grafted onto.

how: The Catholic Church holds an ongoing dialogue with the Jewish people through a Vatican commission for religious relations with the Jews, and popes have visited synagogues. Locally, parishes and synagogues sometimes hold joint study, service and remembrance.

games.q: you're John Paul II, standing in the synagogue of Rome beside its chief rabbi. how do you address the people before you?
o: as strangers you hope to convert.
as your brothers, in a certain way your elder brothers.
games.why: he spoke of them as dearly loved brothers and, in a certain way, elder brothers, words rooted in the council's teaching on the bond with Abraham's stock.

practice: Bring to mind a synagogue in your town, or a Jewish friend, coworker or neighbor, and their week: a Sabbath meal, a school run, a prayer said in Hebrew, a worry you may know nothing about.
If you pray, pray for their peace and safety, in your own simple words or in silence. If you don't, hold them in mind with respect and goodwill.

wordCard.voice: The Jewish people. In Catholic teaching, the people of the covenant God has not revoked, whom a pope called, in a certain way, elder brothers. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: elder brothers. The psalms and the prophets were their prayers first. I'll be here tomorrow.
